claims.text: An on-the-fly machine-learning surrogate potential can replace explicit ab initio molecular dynamics for free-energy evaluation near fusion.
Adaptive sampling of both solid and liquid phases will preserve the accuracy of their free energies.
The surrogate framework can fully retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron-vibration coupling.
Updating surrogate potentials during simulation will accurately capture both solid- and liquid-phase properties without full ab initio molecular dynamics throughout.
Parallel training can produce surrogate potentials that mimic the full interatomic interactions.
The trained surrogate will faithfully reproduce the relevant free-energy surface.
Periodic recalibration against ab initio data will capture the entropy contributions and interaction effects needed for reliable fusion-property predictions.
Replacing most explicit ab initio molecular dynamics with the adaptive surrogate will accelerate free-energy integration while maintaining accuracy.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The proposed method will have accuracy comparable to or better than TOR-TILD for free-energy differences near phase transitions.
TOR-TILD slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The challenges associated with vibrational entropy and anharmonicity are more pronounced in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Prior studies provide preliminary support for machine-learning-based surrogate or predictive training approaches in alloy research.
The cited preliminary support comes from earlier elemental and binary studies.
A deviation greater than approximately 5% in phase free-energy differences or derived observables relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics would falsify the hypothesis.
A speedup of less than one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics would falsify the hypothesis.
